A clean, flat textbook illustration of a Bohr model of an atom. In the centre, a compact nucleus containing red spheres (protons, labelled with '+') and blue spheres (neutrons, blank). Around the nucleus, circular orbits (shells) in dashed lines containing small yellow spheres (electrons, labelled with '-').

Three-dimensional representation of s and p atomic orbitals on x, y, and z axes. On the left, a single spherical s-orbital centered on the origin. On the right, three separate p-orbitals: px (a dumbbell along the x-axis), py (a dumbbell along the y-axis), and pz (a dumbbell along the z-axis).

A chart showing the shapes of simple molecules using ball-and-stick models. 1. Linear: A central grey atom with two green atoms attached at 180 degrees (e.g., CO2). 2. Non-linear (V-shaped): A central red atom (Oxygen) with two smaller white atoms (Hydrogen) attached at an angle of 104.5 degrees. 3. Pyramidal: A central blue atom (Nitrogen) with three white atoms at the base, angled downwards at 107 degrees (NH3). 4. Tetrahedral: A central dark atom (Carbon) with four white atoms arranged at 109.5 degrees in a regular tetrahedron (CH4).
